thread.title: Social Security Faces Shortfall by 2034 Without Congressional Action, Trustees Warn
thread.title_full: Social Security Faces Shortfall by 2034 Without Congressional Action, Trustees Warn

author: Rudy Blalock
title: Social Security Faces Shortfall by 2034 Without Congressional Action, Trustees Warn
text:
Social Security trust funds, which provide benefits to millions of Americans, are projected to run short of money to pay full benefits by 2034 unless Congress intervenes.
2025 OASDI Trustees Report,released Wednesday, shows that this new estimate moves the projected depletion date up by one year compared to last year’s forecast, intensifying the urgency for lawmakers to address the program’s long-term financial challenges.
According to the trustees’ report, Social Security’s trust funds, which support both old-age and disability benefits, will only be able to pay 81 percent of scheduled benefits after 2034 if no legislative changes are made. The depletion date was advanced from last year’s estimate of 2035, reflecting the impact of rising costs and recent legislative changes, including the Social Security Fairness Act.
“Current-law projections indicate that Medicare still faces a substantial financial shortfall that needs to be addressed with further legislation. Such legislation should be enacted sooner rather than later to minimize the impact on beneficiaries, providers, and taxpayers,” the report states.
The Social Security Fairness Act, enacted in January, repealed the Windfall Elimination and Government Pension Offset provisions, increasing benefit levels for certain workers. This change has contributed to the earlier depletion date for the trust funds.
Romina Boccia, director of Budget and Entitlement Policy at the CATO Institute, criticized the move as “a political giveaway masquerading as reform,” arguing that it accelerated the trust fund’s insolvency without addressing the program’s structural imbalances.
Political Challenges and Public Pressure
Efforts to reform Social Security have historically been politically fraught, with lawmakers reluctant to make unpopular changes. President Donald Trump and other Republican leaders have pledged not to cut Social Security or Medicare, even as they seek to reduce overall federal spending.Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano, who took office in May, stated, “The financial status of the trust funds remains a top priority for the Trump Administration,” he said in a June 18 U.S. Department of Treasury press release.
He called on Congress and the Social Security Administration to work together to “protect and strengthen the trust funds for the millions of Americans who rely on it—now and in the future—for a secure retirement or in the event of a disability.”
press release.
Medicare Also Faces Financial Pressure
The trustees’ report also highlighted challenges for Medicare, which provides health insurance to about 68 million Americans, primarily those over 65 or with severe disabilities. The Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund is now projected to be depleted by 2033, three years earlier than last year’s estimate. Once depleted, Medicare would only be able to cover 89 percent of costs for hospital visits and related services.Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. attributed the rising costs to the nation’s focus on “sick care instead of health care,” and highlighted the administration’s Make America Healthy Again agenda to address chronic disease and protect Medicare for future generations, according to the Treasury’s announcement.
The Treasury, which oversees the trust funds, underscored the need for legislative action. “Social Security and Medicare are vital programs that support tens of millions of Americans across the country,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “This data underscores the need for lawmakers to take action to support the long-term viability of these programs”.
Secretary of Labor Lori Chavez-DeRemer added, “Hardworking Americans shouldn’t have to worry about receiving the retirement benefits they’ve earned. Unfortunately, this report shows the combined Social Security trust funds will be depleted by 2034”.
